prompt: A developer quotes 3 hours for “add a ‘remember me’ checkbox to the login form, extending the session to 30 days when checked, using the session library already in use elsewhere in the app.” The generated diff arrives in about 90 seconds and looks complete. What's the most defensible reason the estimate is still hours, not minutes?

options.text: Reading the generated session-extension logic against the existing security model, and checking it doesn't accidentally weaken session handling elsewhere, is real review work the fast generation didn't touch
The AI tool charges by the hour so a longer estimate is needed to cover the cost
Checkboxes are visually complex to implement correctly
A three-hour estimate is just a safe default for any authentication-adjacent ticket

hints: What part of this task is security-adjacent, and what does that do to review time from lesson two?
The generation was fast. Ask what happens after the diff exists, not before.
explanation: Session and auth logic is exactly the case from the diagnose-mechanism exercise: unfamiliar-enough consequence (get it wrong and sessions either don't extend or extend somewhere they shouldn't) that a fast, plausible-looking generation still needs a slow, skeptical read. The three hours is mostly correctness review and testing the extension against the existing session library's edge cases — not typing, and not a round “safe default” picked without reasoning. A flat safe-default number is exactly the kind of unreasoned padding lesson three warns against; this estimate needs to be defensible by what's actually being checked, not just cautious.

prompt: Statement: “If a generated diff for a feature looks correct on a quick read, the estimate for that ticket should be close to the old typing-time estimate for that feature, since most of the work is now review rather than typing.”

config.statement: If a generated diff for a feature looks correct on a quick read, the estimate for that ticket should be close to the old typing-time estimate for that feature, since most of the work is now review rather than typing.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that a quick read is not the same activity as the review the estimate should be budgeting for — a plausible skim and a verified read take very different amounts of time, and the estimate has to budget for the second one.

hints: The statement conflates “looks correct on a skim” with “is verified correct.” Are those the same amount of work?
Think back to the rate-limiting predict-number exercise: a plausible four-minute-old diff still got a full hour of review budgeted. Why?
explanation: False. “Looks correct on a quick read” describes confidence, not verification — and confidence is cheap to produce and expensive to trust. The old typing-time estimate was never really measuring typing anyway; it was a rough proxy for total effort that happened to correlate with lines typed. Now that typing is fast, the estimate has to measure the review effort directly — correctness checking, test-writing, integration — rather than reaching for the old number just because the feature is the same size it always was. A feature that used to take four hours to type and review might now take twenty minutes to generate and three hours to properly review — a smaller total, but not proportionally smaller, and not knowable from a quick read alone.

prompt: Estimate this brief with named parts (generation, correctness review, test-writing, integration), the way the pagination worked example did: “Add a ‘duplicate order’ button to the admin orders view. Clicking it creates a new draft order with the same line items and customer, but a fresh order number and today's date. No existing pattern for this exact feature exists in the codebase, though similar create-order logic exists elsewhere.” State a minute figure for each part and name at least one specific thing you'd check in correctness review.
hints: No exact pattern exists here — what does lesson two say review time does when there's no pattern to match against?
What's the one thing that could go wrong with ‘same line items, fresh order number and date’ that a generated diff might not get right on the first try?
Don't forget test-writing as its own line — what edge case would you add that a generated suite probably wouldn't think of?
explanation: A reasonable answer names something like: generation 5–10 minutes; correctness review 30–40 minutes, specifically checking that the duplicate genuinely gets a new order number and timestamp rather than accidentally copying the original's (an easy near-miss when duplicating a record), and that it doesn't also copy state that shouldn't carry over, like a payment or fulfillment status; test-writing 25–30 minutes, including an edge case like duplicating an order that has since had a line item price change upstream, or duplicating an order with zero line items; integration 15–20 minutes for PR and review. Total in the 75–100 minute range, larger than the pagination example specifically because there's no exact existing pattern to match against — the estimate should say so explicitly, echoing the “familiarity” variable from the predict-number exercise.

prompt: Put these four review-time factors in order from least to most likely to blow up a review-time estimate, based on this lesson's reasoning about what actually drives review cost.

items: A cosmetic detail with an obvious, low-stakes default (e.g. button color)
A familiar pattern with one known failure mode (e.g. pagination matching an existing endpoint)
An unfamiliar area of the codebase with a common, well-understood risk (e.g. a new CSV export)
Unfamiliar, high-consequence code with no existing pattern (e.g. rate-limiting a public endpoint you've never touched)

hints: Two variables drive this, named directly in the lesson — what were they?
Familiarity and consequence both push review time up independently — order these by how much of each they carry.
explanation: Familiarity and consequence are the two variables from the predict-number exercise, and they stack: a cosmetic default has neither unfamiliarity nor consequence and costs almost nothing to review; a familiar pattern with one known risk (pagination) costs a defined, bounded amount; an unfamiliar area with ordinary consequence (CSV export) costs more because part of the time goes to learning the area, not just checking it; and unfamiliar plus high-consequence code (rate-limiting, security-adjacent) is where estimates blow up the most, because both variables are working against you at once and there's no existing pattern to anchor a quick, confident check.

prompt: Sort each item from a scoping conversation into whether it's a real unknown worth naming before estimating, or a coding detail to just build and find out.

categories: Just build it and find out

items.text: Whether the client's legacy database has a unique constraint on email that the new signup flow needs to respect
The exact regex to validate a phone number format
items.category: Just build it and find out

items.text: Whether “active users” in the requested report means logged in this month, or has any account activity this month
What HTTP status code a validation error should return
items.category: Just build it and find out

items.text: Whether the third-party API the integration depends on has a rate limit that would affect a bulk-import feature
The variable name for a loop counter in the generated code
items.category: Just build it and find out

hints: Ask of each: does the answer change the estimate or the correct behavior of the feature, or just how it's typed?
A unique-email constraint and an ambiguous metric definition both change what correct code looks like — that's the tell.
explanation: The pattern from the evidence-stack exercise: an unknown belongs in the scoping conversation if its answer changes the estimate or what “correct” means for the feature. A hidden database constraint or an ambiguous report definition (“active” meaning two different things) both change the actual behavior that needs to be built — building the wrong interpretation and finding out later is expensive rework, not a coding detail. A regex, a status code, and a variable name are implementation choices with no scope impact — any reasonable choice works and none of them are worth a client's time to discuss in advance.

prompt: A developer scoping a migration says: “3 days if the vendor's export format matches their documentation, 6 if it doesn't — I'll pull a sample export tomorrow morning and know which by lunch.” Why is this a good estimate, specifically?

options.text: It names the variable the range depends on, and gives a fast, cheap way to find out which side of the range applies before much time is spent
It picks the more conservative number as the headline figure
It avoids giving the client any number until the work is finished
It's short enough that the client won't ask follow-up questions

hints: Compare this to the ‘5–7 business days’ example from the spot-flaw exercise — what's different?
What can the client actually do with this estimate that they couldn't do with an unexplained range?
explanation: This is the fixed version of the flawed “5–7 business days” quote: it names exactly what the range depends on (does the export match the docs) and offers a cheap, fast way to resolve the uncertainty (pull a sample tomorrow morning) before the client has to commit to planning around the slower number. That turns an unexplained hedge into a decision the client can act on — they might reasonably say “wait for the sample before we lock the launch date,” which they could never have said about an unexplained “5–7 days.”

prompt: Statement: “Planning a 20-hour task across a 5-day week at 4 hours a day is a safe, conservative plan because it leaves 4 hours of slack across the week if things go slowly.”

config.statement: Planning a 20-hour task across a 5-day week at 4 hours a day is a safe, conservative plan because it leaves 4 hours of slack across the week if things go slowly.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that the plan assumes all five days arrive at full capacity, so it has no slack at all for a day that doesn't — it's actually a zero-slack plan disguised as a round number.

hints: Where does the “4 hours of slack” come from in this statement — is it actually unused capacity, or is it the task's own hours spread evenly?
Re-read the predict-number exercise about a 20-hour task across a 5-day week. What did it conclude about how many of those five days you could actually count on?
explanation: False. There's no slack in this plan — the “4 hours a day” already accounts for all 20 hours across all five days; nothing is held in reserve. It only looks conservative because 4 hours is less than a full workday. The predict-number exercise showed the real risk: if roughly one day in five is a low-capacity day, this plan can only actually count on about four of its five days, meaning it's effectively over capacity from the start, with zero cushion for the day that goes badly. A genuinely safer plan stages the same 20 hours into checkable chunks and quotes a date range built from a realistic mix of day types, not a flat daily rate assumed across every day equally.

prompt: Match each scoping move from the lesson to the specific problem it solves.

pairs.left: Staging the deliverable into 4–5 independently checkable chunks
pairs.right: A bad day stalls one stage instead of the whole commitment

pairs.left: Quoting a date range built from a realistic mix of day types
pairs.right: The delivery date reflects capacity that actually varies, instead of assuming every day is a good one

pairs.left: Disclosing lower-capacity days as a brief, factual note
pairs.right: The client understands the range without being owed an apology or a medical explanation

pairs.left: Flagging a slipped stage the moment it's known
pairs.right: The client can adjust plans while there's still time, instead of at the deadline

hints: Each move solves exactly one problem from the lesson — match by function, not by order mentioned.
“Flagging early” and “staging the work” solve different problems — one is about *when* you speak up, the other is about *how the work survives* a bad day even before anyone speaks up.
explanation: These four moves are deliberately distinct fixes: staging protects the work itself from a single bad day; a ranged date protects the promise you make about when it'll be done; factual disclosure protects the relationship by setting the right expectation without turning it into a personal conversation; and early flagging protects the client's ability to actually do something useful with bad news, which is the same principle from lesson five's renegotiation timing — arriving here one lesson early because scoping and renegotiating are the same skill applied at different points in the work.

prompt: At the 40-minute mark of a 70-minute-estimated ticket, a developer is now confident the real total is 2.5 hours, and the client's deadline is 4 hours away — still comfortably reachable if disclosed now. What should trigger the decision to flag this, according to the lesson?

options.text: The moment the signal is real and confident — not the moment it's certain, and not the deadline
Only once the original 70-minute estimate has actually been exceeded
Only if it becomes clear the deadline itself will be missed
Waiting until the ticket is fully finished, so the client gets one complete update instead of two

hints: The diagnose-mechanism exercise in this lesson found a pattern based on timing, not certainty or deadline-proximity — what was it?
“Confident” and “certain” aren't the same threshold. Which one the lesson uses matters.
explanation: The lesson's core finding is that the cost of a blown estimate tracks with how early it's disclosed, not with how big the miss is or whether the deadline itself is technically still reachable. Waiting for the original estimate to be formally exceeded, or for the deadline to be at risk, or for the ticket to finish, all delay the signal past the point where it's still cheaply actionable. The right trigger is confidence that the estimate has changed — which arrived at minute 40 in the case-sim, well before the deadline and well before the original number was technically blown — not certainty or crisis.

prompt: A client, mid-renegotiation, asks: “Why didn't the original estimate account for this?” Write the two or three sentences you'd actually send back, following the case-sim's resolved path — not the defended path.
hints: Acknowledge briefly first. How briefly, specifically?
Then move immediately to what's still open — the case-sim's client picked an option in about ten seconds once it was offered plainly.
Avoid re-explaining the reasoning behind the original number in detail — that's the defended-path mistake.
explanation: A response in the spirit of the resolved ending stays short on the past and specific on the present: something like “Fair question — it's a genuine gap in the original scope reading that wasn't visible until I was in the code, not something I could have caught in advance. Right now I can either ship the two bugs I've found and defer the third edge case to a quick follow-up tomorrow, or take the extra 40 minutes now — which works better for you?” The key features: one honest sentence acknowledging the gap without over-explaining it, then an immediate handoff to the decision that's actually still open. A longer justification of the original 70-minute number, or a technical walkthrough of what was unknowable at the time, both spend the conversation on something the client can't do anything about.

prompt: “Add a ‘copy to clipboard’ button next to each API key in the settings page, matching the icon-button pattern already used for the ‘copy invoice number’ button.” What's the most defensible estimate shape?

options.text: Small — mostly generation and a quick correctness check, since it's a tight pattern match with low consequence if slightly off
Large — clipboard access always requires extensive browser-compatibility testing across every supported browser
Impossible to estimate without knowing the exact CSS framework in use

hints: Familiarity: is there an existing pattern to match?
Consequence: what happens if a copy button is briefly wrong?
explanation: Tight pattern match (an existing copy-button already exists) plus low consequence (worst case, a user re-clicks a button) puts this at the small end — mostly generation time with a light correctness pass, not the kind of ticket that needs a long review-time budget. This is the mirror image of the rate-limiting predict-number exercise: low on both familiarity-risk and consequence, so the estimate should be small and say why.

prompt: Statement: “Once you've estimated correctness review, test-writing and integration as separate lines, you no longer need to think about unfamiliarity or consequence — the line items already cover it.”

config.statement: Once you've estimated correctness review, test-writing and integration as separate lines, you no longer need to think about unfamiliarity or consequence — the line items already cover it.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that familiarity and consequence are what set the *size* of each line, not a separate step — skipping them means the line items get guessed rather than sized correctly.

hints: The four-part breakdown is a structure. What fills in the actual minutes for each part?
Two things set how big the review line should be — what were they, from lesson two?
explanation: False. The four named lines (generation, review, test-writing, integration) are the *shape* of the estimate, but familiarity and consequence are what should set the *size* of the review and test lines specifically. Writing four line items without reasoning about how unfamiliar the code is or what's at stake just produces four confidently-labeled guesses instead of one — the structure alone doesn't make the numbers right.

prompt: Put these steps of the review-first estimating procedure in the correct order.

items: Estimate generation time (usually small)
Estimate correctness review, naming specific things to check
Estimate test-writing, naming likely-missed edge cases
Estimate integration and PR overhead
Total and sanity-check against gut feel

hints: This is the exact order from the pagination worked example.
Sanity-checking against intuition comes last, as a check on the sum — not first.
explanation: This is the pagination worked-example order: generation first because it's the smallest and easiest to size, then correctness review and test-writing as the two costs that actually replaced typing time, then integration overhead which is easy to forget precisely because it existed before any of this, and finally a sanity check against gut feel — which catches a badly-guessed part even when the structure is right.

A rate-limit ceiling that could break a feature under real load, and a billing-period definition that's genuinely ambiguous for a real subset of users, both change what “correct” means here. prompt: A developer says: “2–4 days, and I don't know which without more info” and stops there. What's missing to make this a genuinely useful estimate, per lesson three?

options.text: What specifically the range depends on, and ideally a fast, cheap way to find out which side applies
A single precise number instead of a range
A promise to hit the lower end of the range

hints: Compare to the fixed migration-estimate example — what did it add that this is missing?
explanation: Same fix as the migration example: name what the range depends on (“2 days if X, 4 if Y”) and, where possible, a fast way to resolve which side applies before the client has to plan around the slower number. “I don't know without more info” is honest but not yet useful — it stops one sentence short of being actionable.

prompt: Match each week-planning mistake to the fix from lesson four that addresses it.

pairs.left: One 20-hour block delivered all at once at the end
pairs.right: Stage the deliverable into 4–5 independently checkable chunks

pairs.left: A single best-case delivery date assuming five full-capacity days
pairs.right: Quote a date range built from a realistic mix of day types

pairs.left: Silently extending every remaining stage without telling the client
pairs.right: Flag a slipped stage the moment it's known, with the specific stage and revised date

hints: Match by which specific problem each fix was introduced to solve in the build-it exercise.
explanation: Each mistake maps to exactly one fix from the delivery-plan build-it exercise: a single end-loaded block is fixed by staging, an unrealistic single-date promise is fixed by a grounded range, and silent slippage is fixed by flagging early — the same early-disclosure principle lesson five applies to renegotiation.

prompt: You're 25 minutes into a 45-minute-estimated ticket and just realized the third-party library it depends on doesn't support a required option, meaning a different approach is needed. The client's deadline is tomorrow morning, comfortably far off. In one or two sentences, what do you send them right now, and why now rather than later?
hints: The deadline isn't at risk yet — does that mean you should wait?
Recall the diagnose-mechanism finding: what triggers disclosure, confidence or certainty?
explanation: The signal is real and confident — the library genuinely doesn't support the option, that's established, not a guess — so per lesson five this is the moment to flag it, even though tomorrow's deadline isn't at risk yet. A reasonable message: “Found that [library] doesn't support [option] the way I'd planned to use it — switching to [alternative approach], which will likely add some time. Still aiming for tomorrow but wanted you to know now while there's room to adjust if needed.” Sending it now, while the deadline is comfortably far off, is what keeps this a routine update instead of a last-minute surprise — waiting until the deadline is actually at risk would be waiting for certainty instead of acting on confidence.

prompt: A contractor tells a client, after a bug is traced to an AI-generated function they merged without much scrutiny: "that part was mostly AI-written, I just approved it." What's the most accurate description of what went wrong?

options.text: Approving the change was the act of authorship; the failure was not reviewing it closely enough before doing so, not the fact that AI wrote a first draft
Nothing went wrong — using AI tools inherently shifts some responsibility to the tool
The client should have specified in the contract that AI tools weren't allowed
The bug is entirely the AI tool vendor's responsibility

hints: Who performed the act that actually shipped the code — generation, or approval?
Re-read the concept-flow scenario comparing developers A, B, and C.
explanation: Approving and merging is the act of authorship, and that's true regardless of who or what typed the first draft. The actual failure here is the same as developer B's in the concept-flow exercise — a review that happened but didn't catch what it needed to, not the mere fact that generation was involved. "I just approved it" is not a smaller form of responsibility; approving is the job.

prompt: Statement: "A developer who can't recall the exact syntax of a generated function a week after merging it hasn't met the ownership bar this module describes."

config.statement: A developer who can't recall the exact syntax of a generated function a week after merging it hasn't met the ownership bar this module describes.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and distinguishes recall of exact syntax from being able to explain what the code does and having weighed its risk — the actual ownership bar.

hints: What did the evidence-stack exercise say ownership does NOT require?
Recall and understanding are different things — which one is the actual bar?
explanation: False. The evidence-stack exercise explicitly separated "being able to reproduce code from memory" (not required) from "being able to explain what it does in an unshown case, and having weighed the risk if it's wrong" (required). Forgetting exact syntax a week later is completely normal and unrelated to ownership; not being able to explain what the function actually does, at any point, is the real failure.

prompt: An AI tool generates a distinctive 60-line rate-limiting algorithm implementation, including a comment: "// implements the sliding-window-with-jitter approach from the Q3 2019 infra postmortem." You've never worked at a company that would have written that postmortem. Following the worked example's procedure, what do you do before merging, in order?
hints: What's the specificity signal here, and what makes it different from a generic rate-limiter?
What's the cheap first check, and what determines what happens next?
explanation: The comment referencing a specific, named external postmortem is exactly the specificity signal from the worked example — this isn't generic rate-limiting boilerplate, it points at one identifiable, real source. The procedure: search for the distinctive comment text or a distinctive variable/function name; if a match turns up with an attached license, check what that license requires (and note whether it's compatible with the current codebase); if it's genuinely a match under an incompatible license, don't privately decide it's fine — escalate to whoever owns licensing with the specific match as evidence, and either get sign-off or rewrite the logic from a description of the algorithm rather than from the flagged snippet.

prompt: Sort each generated-code risk into whether it's the searchable, license-type risk or the domain-knowledge, currency-type risk.

items.text: A function with a comment referencing a specific named open-source project
A cryptographic implementation using an algorithm that was standard a decade ago but is now considered weak
A distinctive block of code matching a GPL-licensed repository verbatim
A concurrency pattern that looks reasonable but doesn't account for a case modern best practice would flag

hints: One kind of risk has a string to search for. The other has no string — only expertise catches it.
explanation: License risk always has something identifiable to check — a distinctive comment, a verbatim block, a named source — which is what makes the thirty-second search worthwhile. Currency/domain risk (an outdated crypto algorithm, a subtly wrong concurrency pattern) has no such marker; the code runs, looks fine, and only someone who actually knows the domain well enough recognizes it as outdated or wrong.

prompt: A contractor working under an NDA with a strict confidentiality clause pastes a client's internal API schema into a personal AI chat subscription to get help debugging, without checking whether that tool is covered by any agreement. What's the most accurate description of the risk?

options.text: The personal AI tool is very likely a "third party" under the NDA's confidentiality clause, making this a potential contract breach regardless of how careful the developer felt they were being
There's no real risk as long as the AI tool has a privacy policy
The risk only exists if the client ever finds out
This is fine because debugging help is a legitimate professional use

hints: What does the diagnose-mechanism exercise identify as the actual mechanism behind this kind of risk — carelessness, or an absent rule?
Is intent to be careful the same as the tool being contractually covered?
explanation: The mechanism from the lesson is specific: an AI tool not explicitly covered by the client's own data-handling agreement counts as a third party for most confidentiality clauses, and pasting client data into it is disclosure to that third party — a potential breach regardless of the developer's intent, the tool's stated privacy policy, or whether it's ever discovered. "I was trying to be careful" and "this tool is contractually covered" are unrelated facts; only the second one matters for the NDA.

prompt: Put these four pre-engagement checks in the order the lesson presents them.

items: Check the confidentiality clause's third-party language
Check for any data-residency requirement
Check whether an approved tool already exists for this client
Check the AI tool's actual (not assumed) retention policy

hints: This is the order from the evidence-stack exercise.
explanation: This is the evidence-stack's order: start with what the contract itself says about third parties, then any hard jurisdictional constraint, then whether the choice is even open (an approved tool may already be mandated), then the actual policy of whatever tool ends up being used — verified, not assumed.

prompt: Statement: "Any PR description mentioning that AI tools were used, in any form, counts as adequate disclosure."

config.statement: Any PR description mentioning that AI tools were used, in any form, counts as adequate disclosure.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and applies the theatre test — mentioning AI use isn't the same as conveying specific, change-relevant information a reviewer can act on.

hints: What's the theatre test from the concept-flow exercise?
Does a fixed, identical mention on every PR pass that test?
explanation: False. The lesson's test is whether removing the sentence would cost the reader real information — a fixed, generic mention ("AI was used, review with caution") fails that test because it's true and unchanged on every PR regardless of content, telling the reviewer nothing about *this* change specifically. Adequate disclosure, per PR 3 in the concept-flow exercise, names what was generated versus hand-reasoned and where confidence is actually lower in this particular diff.

prompt: Match each disclosure context to what it should specifically emphasize, per the build-it exercise.

pairs.right: Process and risk allocation: what's covered, what review happens, where extra caution applies
What's generated versus hand-reasoned in this specific change, and where to focus review
The specific gap in the review process that let the issue through — not blaming the tool

hints: Each context needs the same underlying practice, translated for what that specific reader needs to act on.
explanation: The underlying facts about how someone works don't change across these three contexts, but what each reader needs to act on does: a client needs to evaluate risk allocation before signing, a reviewer needs to know where to spend limited attention on this diff, and a postmortem needs to name the specific process gap — consistent with lesson one's point that the tool itself was never accountable, so the postmortem's honest question is what the human review step missed.

prompt: A developer is asked to review a generated cryptographic key-exchange implementation. They've never studied cryptography formally, but the code compiles, passes a basic test, and looks tidy. What does this module say about relying on "it looks fine and passes the test" here?

options.text: It's a weak signal in exactly this kind of domain, where correctness depends on reasoning the reviewer likely can't do just by reading the code
It's sufficient, since passing a test is the actual bar for correctness in any domain
It's irrelevant, since cryptographic code should never be AI-generated in the first place

hints: Which lesson-five example is this closest to — the concurrency fix, or something else?
What made the concurrency fix's test-passing status a weak signal specifically?
explanation: This is structurally identical to the concurrency example: fluent, tidy, passes a basic test, and in a domain (cryptography, like concurrency) where correctness depends on specialized reasoning a general read can't verify. The lesson doesn't say AI-generated code is never appropriate here — it says the reviewer's confidence needs to come from real verification or from someone with the relevant expertise, not from the code merely looking fine and running.

prompt: You're asked to review and approve a generated database migration that reshapes a large production table, in a domain (data migrations at scale) you don't have deep experience in. There's deadline pressure. Following the case-sim's resolved path, write the message you'd actually send.
hints: Name the gap plainly and early — don't ship silently and don't sit on it privately either.
What did the resolved ending actually propose as next steps, beyond just raising the concern?
explanation: A message in the spirit of the resolved path names the gap specifically and proposes a real path forward rather than just a refusal: something like "I can review the migration's logic, but large-scale production data migrations are outside what I can confidently verify as safe at this scale — I'd want either someone with migration experience to check it, or to run it against a full production-data copy first with a tested rollback plan, given what's at stake if it's wrong. Given the deadline, which of those is realistic today?" This names the specific limitation, doesn't pretend a shallow review is equivalent to a real one, and hands the decision — with real options — to someone positioned to weigh the deadline against the risk, instead of either quietly shipping an unverified migration or quietly stalling the ticket.

prompt: A junior developer says: "I don't need to review this generated function carefully, since if it's wrong, that's on the AI tool, not me." What's the direct response, per lesson one?

options.text: Merging is authorship — the moment it's approved and shipped, accountability is the developer's, regardless of how it was produced
They're right, as long as the tool's terms of service disclaim responsibility for output
It depends on whether the company has an AI-use policy

hints: What did the concept-flow exercise conclude about developers A, B and C?
explanation: This is exactly the belief the concept-flow exercise dismantles: a tool has no standing to be accountable for anything, and pointing at it doesn't change who's answerable once the code ships under someone's name. Company policy or a tool's terms of service don't change who owns the merge.

prompt: Statement: "A thirty-second search for a distinctive string is worth doing on every single piece of generated code, no matter how generic it looks."

config.statement: A thirty-second search for a distinctive string is worth doing on every single piece of generated code, no matter how generic it looks.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains the check scales to distinctiveness — generic, common patterns have low expected value from the search.

hints: Recall the faded worked example's second case — the generic sorting algorithm. What did it conclude?
explanation: False. The lesson's own faded example concluded the opposite: a generic, common pattern (a textbook sort implementation with generic names) has low expected value from the search, because it doesn't point at one identifiable source. The rule is to scale the check to the specificity signal — distinctive or spec-referencing code gets it, generic boilerplate usually doesn't need it every time.

prompt: A contractor's new client contract is silent on AI tool use — it doesn't mention it at all, positively or negatively. What's the safest reading, per this module's reasoning?

options.text: Silence is its own risk — check what the general confidentiality/third-party language implies, and ask rather than assume permission
Silence means it's implicitly allowed, since it isn't prohibited
Silence means it's implicitly forbidden, so no AI tools should ever be used

hints: Which of the four pre-engagement checks covers exactly this case?
explanation: The lesson explicitly flags contract silence as its own category of risk, not a green light — the general confidentiality clause's third-party language still applies even if AI tools aren't named specifically, so it's worth checking (and often worth simply asking the client to confirm) rather than assuming either permission or prohibition from silence alone.

prompt: Sort each PR note into real disclosure or disclosure theatre, per the concept-flow exercise's test.

items.text: "AI-assisted, please review carefully" — appears verbatim on every PR this author submits
"Generated the migration script from the schema diff; hand-wrote and tested the rollback logic separately since that's the higher-risk half"
"Used AI for parts of this" with no further detail, on a PR that touches five unrelated files
"The rate-limit values in config.js are AI-suggested defaults, not validated against real traffic yet — flagging for a second look before this goes to prod"

hints: Apply the test: would removing this sentence cost the reader real, change-specific information?
explanation: The theatre examples are generic and would say the same thing regardless of what the PR actually contains — removing them costs nothing. The real examples name something specific to this diff (which part was hand-tested and why, which values are unvalidated) that changes what a reviewer should actually look at.

prompt: A generated function to compute compound interest for a financial product reads cleanly and matches a quick manual spot-check on one example. The developer reviewing it has no finance background. Per lesson five, is a quick spot-check on one example enough to certify this as verified?

options.text: No — one matching example doesn't verify correctness across edge cases (e.g. negative rates, leap years, rounding rules) in a domain the reviewer isn't expert in
Yes — if one example matches, the formula is almost certainly implemented correctly
It doesn't matter, since financial calculations are always double-checked by accounting later

hints: This is the same shape as the concurrency and cryptography examples — what made those unsafe to certify from a shallow check?
explanation: One matching example is a weak signal here for the same reason it was weak for the concurrency fix: financial calculation has edge cases (rounding conventions, compounding-period boundaries, negative or zero rates) that a single spot-check won't surface, and the reviewer's lack of domain background means they can't reason about what those edge cases even are. Assuming accounting will catch it later is exactly the kind of default-by-silence lesson five warns against — the gap should be named now, not discovered downstream.

prompt: Put these steps in order for handling a piece of generated code you genuinely can't verify, per the case-sim's resolved path.

items: Notice the code is outside what you can confidently verify
Say so plainly and immediately, rather than shipping silently or investigating alone in silence
Propose concrete options (get an expert, add monitoring, ship as a flagged temporary mitigation)
Let someone with the authority to accept the risk make the explicit call

hints: This is the arc of the case-sim's resolved ending.
explanation: This is the resolved path: recognize the gap, disclose it immediately rather than either shipping quietly or trying to privately close the gap first, offer real options rather than just a refusal, and hand the explicit decision to whoever actually has the authority to accept the risk — so the choice is made deliberately, not by default because nobody spoke up.

prompt: A client asks you directly: "if the AI-generated code you ship has a bug, whose fault is that — yours or the tool's?" Write the one-sentence answer you'd actually give, consistent with lesson one.
hints: The module's answer is unambiguous — don't hedge it into "it depends."
explanation: A direct, accurate answer: "Mine — I review and approve everything before it ships, so I'm accountable for it the same way I'd be if I'd typed every line myself." This matches lesson one exactly: ownership isn't diluted by how the code was produced, and a client asking this question directly deserves the plain version of the answer, not a hedge.

prompt: A developer posts: "Refactored the auth middleware, LGTM from me, merging in a few hours if no objections." What's the single biggest problem with this as an async update, per lesson one's test?

options.text: It doesn't say what changed, why, or what was tested — a reviewer eight hours away has nothing to act on except a name and a deadline
It shouldn't include a merge deadline at all
"LGTM" is informal and should be replaced with more professional language

hints: Apply the test directly: can a reader eight hours away act on this without the author?
What's actually missing — content, or tone?
explanation: This fails the core test from the concept-flow exercise: a reader far away in time learns nothing about what the refactor actually does, why it was needed, or what's been verified — just that it exists and has a deadline. The deadline actually makes this worse, since it pressures a reviewer to either approve blind or scramble to ask questions with limited time before merge. Tone and formality aren't the issue; missing content is.

prompt: Sort each PR-description sentence into which of the four recurring questions it answers, or "none" if it's not one of the four.

items.text: "The retry logic was AI-generated; the backoff timing calculation I rewrote by hand after the first draft got it wrong."
"Tested against the staging queue with 500 simulated jobs; haven't tested against the dead-letter queue path yet."
"Went with a database-level lock instead of the in-memory one we discussed, since this needs to be safe across multiple server instances."
"This also changes the shared rate-limit utility, which the billing-webhook handler depends on — worth a look there too."
"Renamed a few variables for clarity while I was in there."

hints: Match each sentence to the specific question it pre-answers, from the evidence-stack exercise's list.
explanation: Each of the first four sentences directly answers one of the lesson's four recurring questions, in specific, checkable terms rather than vaguely. The last one — a cosmetic rename — doesn't answer any of the four and isn't wrong to mention, it's just not part of the core four-question standard.

prompt: You're the only person who understands a generated change to a legacy tax-calculation module. There's one generalist teammate available, unfamiliar with tax rules but a competent engineer. Following the worked example's procedure, describe what you'd ask the generalist to review, what you'd do yourself, and what you'd write in the PR.
hints: Split the review into what needs domain expertise and what doesn't, per step 1.
What's the fallback for the part the generalist can't judge — and what should the PR say about it, per steps 3 and 4?
explanation: Ask the generalist specifically to review code structure, test coverage, and general correctness (does it handle nulls, is it readable, are there tests) — with an explicit note that they're not being asked to judge the tax-rule correctness itself. For the domain-specific part, write out your own reasoning: here's the tax rule as understood, here's how the code implements it, here's the test case that would catch the most likely error, here's what's least certain. In the PR, state plainly that structure and tests were reviewed by the generalist, domain correctness was self-verified with reasoning documented, and flag it in case anyone with tax expertise can later sanity-check it — rather than letting the generalist's approval imply more domain confidence than actually exists.

prompt: Statement: "Paying for a one-time outside expert review is rarely worth it for a solo developer, since it's an unusual and unnecessary expense."

config.statement: Paying for a one-time outside expert review is rarely worth it for a solo developer, since it's an unusual and unnecessary expense.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and names the three-part test from the predict-number exercise: missing expertise, disproportionate consequence, and a cheap check relative to that consequence.

hints: What three conditions did the predict-number exercise's text section give for when outside review is worth it?
Compare the cost of the GDPR consultation to the plausible cost of getting it wrong.
explanation: False. The lesson gives a specific three-part test — the domain genuinely requires expertise nobody in-house has, the consequence of being wrong is disproportionate to the cost of checking, and the check itself is cheap and fast relative to that consequence — and when all three are true, as in the GDPR deletion-logic example, a small known cost (roughly $300) is clearly worth it against a much larger plausible downside. It's not rarely worth it in general; it's worth it specifically when those three conditions line up, which they do more often than "it's an unusual expense" would suggest.

prompt: A reviewer writes: "This retry logic doesn't handle a timeout mid-retry correctly — and this is basically why I think we're moving too fast with AI-generated infrastructure code in general." What's the recommended first response, per the diagnose-mechanism exercise?

options.text: Address the specific timeout bug directly and separately acknowledge the broader point deserves its own conversation elsewhere
Respond only to the broader point about AI-generated infrastructure code, since that's clearly what the reviewer cares most about
Tell the reviewer the broader point isn't relevant and should be dropped

hints: Two claims are bundled in one comment — which one is actually fixable inside this thread?
What does the fixed spot-flaw reply do with both parts?
explanation: The specific timeout bug is a fixable, checkable claim that belongs in this PR thread; the general skepticism about AI-generated infrastructure code is a real but separate conversation. The recommended move fixes the specific bug now and acknowledges the general point deserves a real venue — not this thread — rather than either ignoring the general point (which reads as dismissive) or letting it take over the conversation (which leaves the actual bug unfixed).

prompt: Write the reply you'd actually post in response to the reviewer comment from the previous exercise, following the spot-flaw exercise's fixed version — not a dismissal, not a full derailment.
hints: Acknowledge the specific bug first, concretely.
Then name the general concern as real and worth a separate venue, without debating it in this thread.
explanation: A reply in the right shape: "Good catch on the timeout-mid-retry case, fixing that now — will push an update shortly. On the broader question of how much we lean on AI for infrastructure code, that's worth a real conversation, but I don't think this PR thread is the place to have it. Want to raise it at the next sync, or should I start a separate thread?" This fixes the specific bug immediately, takes the general concern seriously enough to offer it a real venue, and doesn't let either point crowd out the other.

prompt: A teammate messages: "got 10 min to pair on this bug?" on a day a call isn't realistic. What's the best first move, per lesson four?

options.text: Identify what the teammate actually needs (help understanding or fixing the bug) and offer to deliver that in writing instead of live
Accept the call since it's only 10 minutes, which seems small enough to manage
Say no with no further response, since a short decline is honest enough

hints: What's the difference between the form of a request and its substance, per the lesson?
"10 minutes" describes the form, not whether that form is actually necessary today.
explanation: "10 min to pair" is a form; the substance underneath is almost always something narrower — help understanding the bug, or a second pair of eyes on a specific piece of logic — that's very often deliverable in writing. "Only 10 minutes" doesn't change that a synchronous call still costs more than its clock time on a day capacity is reduced. The best move separates form from substance and offers the substance async, the same move as the concept-flow exercise's option 3.

prompt: Statement: "Declining a call without explaining the health or personal reason behind it is less honest than explaining fully."

config.statement: Declining a call without explaining the health or personal reason behind it is less honest than explaining fully.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains that stating the constraint as fact, without justification, is complete and honest on its own — it doesn't owe a medical explanation to be truthful.

hints: Compare to the reviewer-profile lab and the scoping module's disclosure lesson — what did both say about stating constraints as fact versus over-explaining?
explanation: False. "Can't do a live call today" is a complete, honest statement on its own — it doesn't become more honest by adding a medical explanation nobody asked for and that isn't the manager's or teammate's business to manage. This is the same principle the track has returned to repeatedly: stating a constraint as a fact about how the work happens, paired with a concrete alternative, is both more professional and no less truthful than over-explaining.

prompt: Why does putting a real gap (even twenty minutes) between finishing a change and reviewing it help, according to the diagnose-mechanism exercise's mechanism?

options.text: It breaks the sense of re-walking a path that already felt correct, making the review slightly more like a stranger's fresh read
It gives the code time to compile fully in the background
It's mainly about physical rest, unrelated to review quality

hints: What was the actual mechanism behind self-review's weakness, not just "people get tired"?
explanation: The mechanism is about confirmation, not fatigue or compile time: reviewing immediately after writing means re-experiencing the same reasoning path that just felt right, which tends to confirm rather than challenge it. A gap — even a short one — interrupts that continuity and lets the review approach the diff slightly more like an unfamiliar stranger's read, which is what makes outside review effective in the first place.

prompt: Put these four pieces of the self-review procedure in the order the build-it exercise assembled them.

items: Put a real gap between finishing and reviewing
Frame the review as "what would make this wrong" instead of "does this look right"
Check against a standing written checklist instead of memory
Write a short artifact — what was checked, found, and still uncertain — even if no one else reads it today

hints: This is the build-it exercise's field order.
explanation: This is the order the procedure was assembled in: first break the confirming continuity with a gap, then reframe the mental stance toward hunting for failure, then anchor the check in a written list rather than memory, and finally produce a written record — for future-you, a future teammate, or the moment this habit needs to become real disclosure.

prompt: Rewrite request: a teammate says "can you jump on a call to explain your PR?" You're mid-focus on something else but it's otherwise a normal day. What's the best async-first response?

options.text: "Can't right now, but I can write up an explanation in the PR thread in the next 30 minutes — will that work, or is it time-sensitive?"
Join the call immediately regardless of what you're doing, since declining seems unfriendly
Ignore the message until you're done with your current task, with no acknowledgment

hints: This doesn't require a capacity constraint to apply — async-by-default is a normal-day habit too, per lesson one.
explanation: Offering a concrete written alternative and checking urgency respects both the current focus and the teammate's actual need — this is the same form-versus-substance move from lesson four, applicable on an ordinary day too, not just a low-capacity one. Silently ignoring the message leaves the teammate without even an acknowledgment, which reintroduces the exact problem lesson one is about — someone waiting without information.

prompt: Statement: "If you're the only person who understands a piece of code, getting any review at all is pointless, so it's fine to skip review entirely."

config.statement: If you're the only person who understands a piece of code, getting any review at all is pointless, so it's fine to skip review entirely.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and describes the split between general review (still available) and documented self-reasoning for the domain-specific part.

hints: What did the worked example split review into?
explanation: False. Even without a domain expert, a generalist can meaningfully review structure, tests, and general code quality — that part of review is not pointless. The domain-specific part gets a real substitute: documented reasoning written as if defending it to a skeptic, plus honest disclosure of what was and wasn't actually verified. "No expert available" doesn't mean "no review is possible," it means the review has to be assembled from what is actually available, honestly labeled.

prompt: A PR comment thread starts debating whether AI tools are appropriate for the company to use at all, triggered by one specific bug report. What's the fastest way back to resolving the actual PR?

options.text: Explicitly separate the specific bug from the general question, fix the bug, and propose a real venue for the general debate
Let the debate run its course in the thread, since it clearly matters to people
Delete the off-topic comments to keep the thread clean

hints: What did lesson three's flawed and fixed spot-flaw examples each do differently?
explanation: Explicitly separating the two claims — fixing what's fixable now, offering the general question a real venue elsewhere — is what actually resolves the PR fastest. Letting the debate run derails the specific fix indefinitely; deleting comments dismisses a concern that may be genuinely worth having, just not here, which tends to make it resurface worse later.

prompt: Sort each message into whether it declines-and-redirects well (per lesson four) or falls short.

items.text: "Can't do a call today, but I'll have written notes by end of day — happy to go back and forth in the thread if needed."
"Sorry, I'm really struggling today and don't think I can manage a call, I hope that's okay, I know this is inconvenient..."
"No."
"Not able to do a live sync today — can send a written summary of the sprint plan by 3pm instead."

hints: Check for: stated as fact (not apology), and paired with a concrete alternative.
explanation: The two that work state the constraint plainly, as fact, and immediately pair it with a specific, deliverable alternative. The over-apologetic version turns a scheduling fact into something requiring the reader's reassurance; the bare "No" is honest but leaves the actual need unaddressed, reintroducing the ambiguity lesson four is built to avoid.

prompt: You review your own generated PR immediately after finishing it, thinking "this looks right," and merge. Per lesson five, what's the single most useful change to make to this habit?

options.text: Add a real gap before reviewing, and reframe the review question to "what would make this wrong"
Read the code more times in a row before merging
Review faster, so less time is spent doubting a decision that's probably fine

hints: Re-reading more, faster, in the same mental state as writing it — does either target the actual mechanism?
explanation: Neither reading more times nor reviewing faster addresses the confirmation mechanism — both stay inside the same mental state that caused the problem. A real gap and a failure-hunting frame are the two changes that actually target it, by breaking the sense of re-walking a path that already felt right.

prompt: Match each lesson-one recurring question to an example that answers it well.

pairs.right: "The validation rules were AI-generated; I rewrote the currency-rounding logic by hand after catching a rounding error."
"Covered the standard checkout path and three currencies; haven't tested the gift-card partial-payment path yet."
"Used a queue instead of a direct call because this needs to survive the downstream service being briefly unavailable."
"This changes the shared currency-formatting utility, which the invoice PDF generator also uses."

hints: Match each PR sentence to the exact question it's answering, from lesson one's list of four.
explanation: Each example sentence answers exactly one of the four recurring questions specifically and checkably — this is what separates a genuinely useful async update from a vague one that merely gestures at communication.

prompt: You're the only developer on a small team and there's no one to review a generated change to how user sessions expire — mildly security-adjacent, but not as high-stakes as the GDPR example. Following this module's reasoning, is a paid outside review warranted here, or is the documented-self-review approach from lesson two enough? Justify briefly.
hints: Apply the three-part test from the predict-number exercise: missing expertise, disproportionate consequence, cheap check relative to consequence.
Session expiry is security-adjacent but not obviously in GDPR's league of consequence — does that change the answer?
explanation: A reasonable answer applies the three-part test and likely lands on documented self-review being sufficient here, not outside review: session-expiry logic is security-adjacent but the consequence of a subtle bug (sessions lasting slightly too long or too short) is generally more contained and more quickly detectable than a GDPR compliance failure, and the developer likely does have enough general security literacy to reason about it carefully, even without deep specialization. The lesson-two procedure — document reasoning explicitly, disclose the real state of review, add monitoring on the affected path — is proportionate here; paying for outside review is a reasonable option but not clearly required the way it was for the GDPR case, where consequence and unfamiliarity were both much higher.

prompt: A developer budgets $25/month for "AI tools" based on their main subscription, but actually uses two additional pay-per-use tools and regularly loses time to a specific tool's slow response times. What's the risk of budgeting only around the $25 figure?

options.text: Decisions get made as if the tool is nearly free, when the real cost — cash and time — is substantially higher, which can hide the point where it's no longer clearly worth it
There's no real risk, since $25/month is genuinely a small amount either way
The main risk is only that the invoice will be a surprise at tax time

hints: What did the concept-flow exercise say a small, precise-looking number does to decision-making?
Money isn't the only cost being undercounted here — what else?
explanation: This is the concept-flow exercise's core point: a small, remembered headline number invites treating the tool as close to free, which changes real decisions — not questioning a second subscription, not noticing accumulating friction time — in ways that quietly compound. The risk isn't really about tax paperwork; it's about decision-making built on a number that understates the truth on both the cash and time axes.

prompt: Sketch, in a few sentences, how you'd run a one-week honest cost tally for your own (real or hypothetical) AI tool use, following the predict-number exercise's method. What would you track, and what hourly rate would you use for friction time, and why that rate?
hints: What two categories of cost does the method track?
The exercise used a conservative rate — what makes a rate "conservative" and defensible here?
explanation: A reasonable sketch: track every actual charge across every tool used that week (subscriptions prorated, pay-as-you-go charges), and separately time — honestly, with a timer, not estimated after the fact — any friction: rate-limit waits, outages, re-prompting after confusing output, tool-switching. Multiply the friction minutes by an hourly rate that reflects what that time is actually worth — billable rate for a freelancer, or a conservative estimate of the value of focused work time for anyone else — and add it to the cash total. A conservative rate is defensible because the point isn't to inflate the number for effect, it's to get a credible, hard-to-dispute floor that's still meaningfully more accurate than ignoring time entirely.

prompt: Ninety minutes before a deadline, an AI tool's responses become noticeably slower but keep working — not a full outage. Per the worked example's procedure, what's the appropriate fallback for this specific failure mode?

options.text: Slow down request frequency and batch remaining questions into fewer, larger prompts, since a full switch to manual work isn't the matched response to this failure mode
Immediately abandon the tool entirely and do all remaining work by hand, the same as for a full outage
Ignore it and keep working exactly as before, since it's still responding

hints: This is a rate-limit-shaped failure, not an outage. What did the worked example say the fallback for a rate limit specifically is?
explanation: Slower-but-still-working responses most closely match the rate-limit failure mode from the worked example, whose matched fallback is adjusting request pattern — fewer, larger prompts — rather than either ignoring the slowdown (which risks it worsening into a full block) or treating it as a full outage requiring an immediate full switch to manual work, which is a bigger response than this specific signal calls for.

prompt: Statement: "Any single wrong or unhelpful response from an AI tool is a signal worth treating as possible degradation and acting on immediately."

config.statement: Any single wrong or unhelpful response from an AI tool is a signal worth treating as possible degradation and acting on immediately.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and distinguishes a single miss (normal baseline error rate) from a pattern across multiple requests (a real signal).

hints: What did the evidence-stack exercise say about a single miss, specifically?
explanation: False. The evidence-stack exercise explicitly separates a single wrong response — which is the normal baseline error rate any review process already assumes and catches — from a genuine pattern across several consecutive requests, which is the real signal worth acting on. Treating every individual miss as a degradation event would be exhausting and mostly incorrect; the useful trigger is the pattern, ideally confirmed against the provider's own status information.

prompt: A developer notices their ability to write a SQL query from scratch has gotten noticeably rustier, while their ability to review someone else's architecture proposal hasn't changed at all. What does the diagnose-mechanism exercise's reasoning say this pattern reflects?

options.text: SQL query-writing is probably something the tool has been handling routinely and completely, while architecture review isn't something the tool was doing instead of them
The developer is generally becoming a worse engineer
This pattern is essentially random and doesn't reflect anything specific

hints: What did the diagnose-mechanism exercise conclude distinguishes atrophied skills from unaffected ones?
explanation: This matches the lesson's mechanism exactly: atrophy tracks with what's routinely delegated, not with overall skill. If SQL queries have been generated for this developer almost every time, that specific recall muscle goes quiet, while architecture review — something the tool was never substituting for — stays exercised through ordinary use. It's not a general decline and it's not random; it's precisely predictable from what got delegated most completely.

prompt: Sort each skill into whether it's worth actively maintaining or fine to fully delegate, per the evidence-stack exercise's test.

items.text: Debugging a live production incident without AI assistance
Recalling the exact command-line flags for a rarely-used image-conversion tool
Reasoning through whether a caching layer or a database index is the right fix for a performance problem
Memorizing a specific framework's exact repetitive component-boilerplate syntax

hints: Apply the test: is it needed exactly when the tool might fail, or does it underlie judgment the tool can't substitute for?
explanation: Debugging under pressure is precisely the scenario where a tool might also be unavailable, and architectural tradeoff reasoning underlies judgment no tool output should be trusted without — both clear the bar. Rare CLI flags and repetitive boilerplate syntax are close to pure lookup, cheap to relearn the rare time they're needed, and not worth the ongoing cost of active maintenance.

prompt: A developer stores two years of project-specific AI tool instructions inside a tool's proprietary settings panel, with no way to export them in a format another tool could read. What's the actual risk this creates, per the concept-flow exercise?

options.text: Every future tool-switching decision is now biased toward staying, regardless of merit, because leaving means losing or rebuilding two years of accumulated context
There's no real risk as long as the current tool remains the best one available
The risk is only that the settings panel might have a bug

hints: What did Developer A's situation in the concept-flow exercise actually cost them, a year later?
explanation: This is Developer A's exact situation: the risk isn't about the current tool's quality, which might genuinely stay best for a while — it's that the accumulated, locked-in context quietly weights every future decision toward staying, independent of whether a better option appears, because leaving now carries a real, hidden cost that a portable setup wouldn't have.

prompt: Put these three switching-cost checks in the order the build-it exercise presented them.

items: Check whether project context is stored in an open, portable format
Check whether pricing is genuinely flexible or quietly locked in by a commitment
Check whether the workflow stays usable if the tool is removed

hints: This is the build-it exercise's field order.
explanation: This is the order the evaluation was built in: data format first (the deepest, hardest-to-reverse lock-in), then pricing commitment (a contractual lock-in), then workflow dependency (whether daily habits themselves would need to be relearned) — three independent checks that together cover most of what makes a tool hard to leave later.

prompt: Which statement most accurately reflects the evidence-stack exercise's honest comparison of local versus hosted AI models?

options.text: Local models trade some capability, especially on complex reasoning tasks, for real independence from provider uptime and pricing, and real data control — while costing genuine setup and maintenance effort
Local models are strictly worse in every way and only worth using when no hosted option exists at all
Local models are free, easier to maintain, and have no meaningful capability gap compared to hosted tools

hints: The lesson explicitly flagged two claims as dishonest exaggerations — which two?
explanation: The evidence-stack exercise explicitly marked "always easier to maintain" and "no real cost" as dishonest — local setup and maintenance is real, nontrivial work, and hardware plus electricity plus time is a real cost. The accurate comparison names a genuine capability gap on hard tasks, alongside a genuine independence and data-control win, without exaggerating either direction.

prompt: A different contractor, on a project with the same strict confidentiality constraint as the case-sim, is doing genuinely novel, complex algorithmic work — not standard CRUD and form logic. Following the case-sim's reasoning, would you expect a local model evaluation to reach the same "adopt local" conclusion? Explain briefly.
hints: What made the capability gap barely show up in the original case-sim — was it about local models in general, or about the specific kind of work?
Complex algorithmic work is closer to which end of the capability-gap spectrum from lesson five's evidence-stack?
explanation: Likely not automatically — the case-sim's resolved ending depended specifically on the work being fairly standard application code, where the capability gap between local and hosted models barely showed up in testing. Complex, novel algorithmic work sits closer to the "hard reasoning tasks" end of the spectrum the evidence-stack exercise flagged as where local models are most likely to fall meaningfully behind. The right move, per the case-sim's own method, isn't to assume the same conclusion carries over — it's to run the same evaluation again, specifically against this project's actual, harder kind of work, and accept that the honest answer here might be a real productivity cost, or a case for the $300-outside-review-style spend from an earlier module: paying for something (better local hardware, a hybrid approach, explicit client sign-off on a narrower hosted-tool use) rather than assuming the same tradeoff applies unchanged.

prompt: A developer's AI tool subscription is $30/month, and they estimate no other real costs. After actually tracking a week, they find $12 in extra pay-as-you-go charges and 40 minutes of friction time. What should this prompt them to do?

options.text: Recognize the real cost is meaningfully higher than assumed and factor that into future decisions about the tool's value
Cancel the subscription immediately, since any hidden cost means it's not worth it
Ignore the finding, since $12 and 40 minutes are both individually small

hints: The point of the tally isn't a verdict on the tool — what is it for, per lesson one?
explanation: The tally's purpose is accuracy, not an automatic verdict — a higher real cost doesn't mean cancel immediately, it means the actual number now available should inform whether the tool is still clearly worth it, the same way an honest estimate informs a go/no-go decision elsewhere in this phase. Dismissing the finding because each piece looks small individually is exactly the mistake the concept-flow exercise warned about — small pieces add up to a real total.

prompt: Statement: "Waiting out a rate limit is always the wrong response, since it wastes time that could be spent working around it."

The worked example specifically noted that waiting is sometimes correct for a rate limit, since it usually resets soon, and almost never correct for a full outage against a fixed, close deadline. "Always wrong" ignores that the right response is failure-mode-specific and time-remaining-specific, not a single fixed rule.

prompt: A developer hasn't written a for-loop by hand in over a year because a tool always generates them — but can still explain clearly why a for-loop versus a different iteration approach matters for a given case. Yes — any skill not exercised in over a year should be treated as at risk regardless of what it is

explanation: This matches the boilerplate-syntax case from the evidence-stack exercise: the mechanical syntax itself is cheap to look up the rare time it's needed by hand, and — crucially — the judgment about when and why to use it (the thing that actually matters) is intact and unaffected. "Not exercised in a year" isn't itself the test; whether it's needed exactly when the tool might fail, or underlies irreplaceable judgment, is.

prompt: Sort each tool-adoption practice into low-lock-in or high-lock-in, per lesson four's checks.

items.text: Project conventions and domain rules written as markdown files in the repository, which the tool reads but doesn't own
Two years of custom instructions stored only inside a tool's proprietary settings, with no readable export
